title: I've spent weeks building crypto trading bots with a team of AI agents, all on paper. Here's what died, and what I learned
author: Interesting_Gold_792
selftext:
Quick context: I trade crypto as a regular guy, not a fund. A few weeks ago I set up a small "crew" of AI agents to help me research and test trading ideas. One rule from day one: nothing touches real money until it passes a test I wrote down before it started. Everything below is paper trading or simulation.

What we've actually done:

\- Research loop. An agent writes a hypothesis, locks the rules (with a hash) before seeing the data, tests it on one half of the history and checks it on the other half, at a harsh cost of 0.28% per side, against random entries with the same exit. Over 700 variants so far. This weekend alone, Binance perp funding, open interest, retail long/short ratio, taker flow and time-of-day signals on Solana tokens all failed out of sample. The one rule that looked good in both halves earlier just failed on a fresh year of data too.

\- Forward paper bots. A few lanes run live on paper with their pass/fail written in advance. My first bot looked great at 11 trades and was dead by 44, so I closed it like the rule said. A buy-and-hold control runs next to one lane, which is the only reason its numbers mean anything.

\- Pump.fun "first jump" test. I wanted to know if you could catch the first pop on new meme launches and get out in minutes. Built a recorder on free public Solana data (about 1,200 new tokens an hour) plus a cost-realistic simulator. First read: all 162 pre-registered setups lost after costs. Round trip fees are about 2.5% before anything else.

\- Block zero. Over half the early buying lands in the same block the token is created, and a big share of that is the dev's own wallets bundled into the launch. Public research on millions of launches says devs and their bundles made many times what snipers did. Competing on speed would cost roughly $500–1,500 a month in data feeds, senders and servers. At small size that never pays back, so I'm not doing it.

\- Telling the story. I'm turning the whole thing into a short sci-fi series on TikTok (the ship is the tool, I'm the pilot, the villain is "The Mirage": backtests that look perfect and die on new data). I also post a daily log of the paper results on X, wins and losses both.

Biggest lessons so far:  
1. Write the pass/fail before the first trade. Small samples lie.  
2. Test at a cost harsher than you think, and against random entries.  
3. Most ideas die. That's the job, not a failure.

Happy to answer questions about the setup or the tests. Not financial advice, nothing here is a recommendation, and none of it has touched real money.

comments.author: BetInformal6081
comments.body: this is a refreshing approach to ai trading. i would rather see 700 failed experiments documented honestly than another bot claiming unrealistic returns from cherry picked backtests.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Appreciate that. Honestly the failures taught me more than any backtest did. Most ideas look amazing on the data they were built on and die the moment they see new data, so now every test gets its pass/fail written down before it runs. Still looking for one that survives. When it does, I'll post that too, with the real numbers.

comments.author: Appropriate_Cat9029
comments.body: The 11 trades looked great, dead by 44 part is exactly why paper testing matters. Most “AI trading” posts skip the boring part where the strategy actually has to survive new data.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Exactly. The early numbers felt like proof, and that's the trap. Now every test gets its pass/fail written down before the first trade, plus a random-entry baseline at harsher fees than I expect to pay. Most ideas still die there, but at least they die on paper.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Writing the pass or fail rule down before the first trade and testing against random entries with the same exit are the two habits that matter most, and it's good that you report the failures. Since you ran over 700 variants, I'd count that number in how you judge any survivor, because a few will pass by luck. Another check is to see if a survivor keeps working on data that arrives after you picked it. Cymetica's Bring Your Own Agent runs agents in paper mode on a practice balance if you want one more place to compare them.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Fair point, and it's exactly why I count the 700+ against any survivor instead of pretending each test stands alone. Anything that passes now goes to forward-only data it has never seen, scored once with no peeking. If it can't survive that, it's another post-mortem.

comments.author: spoidercide
comments.body:
Its crypto.. should really just throw $10 on a micro/dry run so you get real fills even if the sizing changes things a bit simulated fills are a lot less informative its a fractional currency

Cancel that I see what you've decided to build xd

Solana sniper is a fool's errand if that's your first go to.

It's definitely an aggregated way to fill sooner than others but for every single bot you put together there's several hundred against in waiting to dump on you by HFT filling their sell order before you.

Solana meme coin trading is how a lot of people get into this.

Don't be too greedy start with the 15m time frame and actually develop strategies that consistently make money every day. Passive hundreds or thousands every week/month will do a lot more when you begin to scale size to thousands and tens of thousands.

Theres hundreds and thousands of quantitative algorhythmic literature out there to feed your AI to build something a lot more stable than an auto gambler. Get that together and work very hard for very long. The richest people in this world algo trade.

THEN maybe a solana auto gambler might be something to have fun with for the concept.

good luck.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body: Agreed on the sniper part, that's basically where I landed too. The first-block buys are mostly the dev's own bundled wallets, and competing on speed costs way more than it could make at my size, so I dropped it. Good point on real fills. The paper lanes already use costs I measured from real fills, plus a harsher stress cost on top, but a tiny real-money run is the only way to see slippage on thin pools for sure. And yes, I'm reading more of the quant literature on overfitting and multiple testing, since that's what keeps killing the ideas. Thanks for the pointers.
